summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing IEEE 802.3 repeaters running at 10 and 100 megabits per second, using the SMIv2 format. It lets network management software monitor and control repeater devices.

eli5.summary: A dashboard with standard dials so a manager can check on the small signal-boosting boxes in a network.

questions: how does snmp monitor ethernet repeaters
what changed from rfc 1516 to rfc 2108
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and controlling IEEE 802.3 10 and 100 Mb/s repeaters, hubs and stacks.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a standard way to monitor and control Ethernet repeaters, including multi-repeater systems and 100 Mb/s devices, which the earlier repeater MIB did not cover.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines SNMP-REPEATER-MIB in SMIv2 with packages for basic status and control, monitoring counters, address tracking and search, and TopN reports, based on IEEE 802.3 Section 30.
tldr.outcome: It is a superset of RFC 1516, which it replaces, and adds support for multiple repeaters, 100BASE-T, port TopN and topology mapping.

today: RFC 2108 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1516, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: What the Repeater MIB Covers
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing IEEE 802.3 10 and 100 Mb/s baseband repeaters, based on IEEE Std 802.3 Section 30, "10 & 100 Mb/s Management". It is written for the SNMP Network Management Framework, which consists of the SMI (RFC 1902), MIB-II (RFC 1213) and an access protocol. Objects are named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER and described in the subset of ASN.1 defined in the SMI.

The objects represent attributes of repeaters as defined in Section 9 (10 Mb/s) and Section 27 (100 Mb/s) of the IEEE standards. The counters are defined to be the same as those in the IEEE document, so the same instrumentation can serve both the IEEE and IETF management standards. The MIB may also be used for non-standard repeater-like devices, but objects for their implementation-specific properties are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Many makers build the same kind of signal-boosting box. This memo gives all of them the same set of labelled dials so one program can read any of them.

sections.title: Repeaters, Ports and MIB-II
sections.content:
A repeater is a bitwise store-and-forward device. It recognizes activity and bits but does not process data using packet information such as checksums or addresses. It has no MAC address, no MAC implementation, and does not pass packets up to higher protocol entities.

Because of that, the MIB-II interfaces group does not apply to a repeater's ports. A MIB-II interface has no specific relationship to a repeater port. The interfaces group applies only to the network interfaces over which the managing entity sends and receives management operations. The memo assumes a repeater implementing this MIB also implements at least the MIB-II system group.

The module defines terms such as repeater-unit (the part inboard of the physical media interfaces), group (an optional entity supporting modular port numbering, such as field-replaceable units), chassis, module and stack.
sections.eli5: A repeater only echoes signals and never reads the letters inside. So it has no street address of its own, and the manager reaches it through a different door.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
Objects are arranged into four packages under snmpDot3RptrMgt, which is { mib-2 22 }. The packages are for organizational convenience only and have no relation to the conformance groups defined later.

  • Basic (1): status, parameter and control objects for each repeater, the port groups and the individual ports.
  • Monitor (2): statistics for each repeater and for individual ports.
  • Address tracking (3): tracking the MAC addresses of attached devices and mapping the network topology.
  • TopN (4): tracking the ports with the most activity.

Some subtrees are marked as currently unused, such as the group-level address tracking and the repeater-level and group-level TopN subtrees.

The address tracking definitions are based on a technology patented by Hewlett-Packard, which has granted rights to implementors of this MIB.
sections.eli5: The control panel is split into four drawers: basics, counters, who-is-plugged-where, and who-is-busiest.

sections.title: Basic Repeater, Group and Port Control
sections.content:
The new rptrInfoTable holds one row per managed repeater and is the preferred source of repeater-level information. It includes rptrInfoRptrType, which identifies the repeater as other, 10 Mb, 100 Mb Class I or 100 Mb Class II. The older scalar objects under rptrRptrInfo exist for backward compatibility with RFC 1516 implementations and duplicate the first row of that table.

Each port has an rptrPortAdminStatus (enabled or disabled), an rptrPortAutoPartitionState and an rptrPortOperStatus. A disabled port neither transmits nor receives and stays disabled across power loss or reset until explicitly enabled. Admin status takes precedence over auto-partition. Enabling a port starts its auto-partition state machine, and its auto-partition state becomes notAutoPartitioned. rptrPortRptrId says which repeater a port belongs to, and zero means none.
sections.eli5: Each plug on the box has an on/off switch and a light that says whether the box has temporarily cut it off for misbehaving.

sections.title: Monitoring Counters and TopN Reports
sections.content:
The monitor package keeps per-port counters taken from the IEEE definitions, including readable frames and octets, FCS errors, alignment errors, frames too long, short events, runts, collisions, late events, very long events, data rate mismatches, auto-partitions and total errors. A separate 100 Mb/s table adds isolates and symbol errors, plus optional upper-32-bit and 64-bit high-capacity octet counters. Repeater-level and group-level totals are also defined.

Counter descriptions often cite IEEE timings. For example, a short event is a carrier event shorter than ShortEventMaxTime, which is greater than 74 and less than 82 bit times. The text notes an approximate minimum rollover of 16 hours for some counters in a 10 Mb/s repeater, and many counters note a possible discontinuity when rptrMonitorPortLastChange changes.

The TopN package lets a management station create a row in rptrTopNPortControlTable choosing a repeater, a statistic (the rate base), a duration and a requested size. When the report is ready, static rows appear in rptrTopNPortTable ranking the ports by the rate of that counter.
sections.eli5: The box keeps tally marks for every kind of hiccup on each plug. A manager can also ask which plugs were busiest or most troubled over a stretch of time.

sections.title: Address Search and Topology Mapping
sections.content:
Address tracking lets a manager find which port a MAC address was heard on. Each repeater has one row in rptrAddrSearchTable, and only one address search can run per repeater at a time. A manager first takes ownership using the TestAndIncr semantics of rptrAddrSearchLock together with rptrAddrSearchStatus and rptrAddrSearchOwner. If its set fails, another manager got the lock and it retries. It then sets rptrAddrSearchAddress, waits for rptrAddrSearchState to leave none, and if the state is single reads the group and port. Finally it releases the entry by setting the lock to its previous value plus one. The agent resets an entry stuck in use after an abnormally long time, and the memo suggests one to five minutes.

Section 4 of the memo describes how a management system can use this to map topology. Pick a device, see on which of its ports every other device is heard, and treat each port as a temporary segment. Then recursively let devices in each segment eliminate others: a device is removed from the segment if a child hears the parent on one port and that device on another. Workstations are placed the same way. For bridges and switches the Bridge MIB forwarding database provides the address-to-port association, and for repeaters the rptrAddrSearchTable does.
sections.eli5: To find which plug a computer is on, the manager asks the box to listen for it. Only one person may ask at a time, so there is a take-a-number lock. Asking every box where everyone is lets a program draw the whole network map.

sections.title: Relationship to RFC 1516
sections.content:
This MIB is intended as a superset of RFC 1516, which "will go to historic status". It contains all RFC 1516 objects plus new ones for multiple repeaters, 100BASE-T management, port TopN, and address search and topology mapping. Implementors are encouraged to support all applicable conformance groups.

Some objects are deprecated. The single-repeater scalars such as rptrOperStatus, rptrReset and the rptrHealth and rptrResetEvent notifications are marked deprecated because the multiple-repeater definitions duplicate them, and others were deprecated based on implementation experience. The newer rptrInfoHealth and rptrInfoResetEvent notifications take their place. The deprecated notifications must be throttled to at least five seconds apart, and throttled traps are dropped, not queued.
sections.eli5: This is the new, bigger version of an older control panel. All the old dials still work, but a few were replaced by better ones.

sections.title: Conformance Groups
sections.content:
The module ends with object groups and three compliance statements, covering the earlier RFC 1368 and RFC 1516 versions and the current one. For a system with one or more repeater-units, the current compliance requires the basic, monitor and address tracking groups. The 100 Mb/s monitor group is mandatory for systems with 100 Mb/s repeaters, and the 64-bit counter group for those that can also support Counter64.

The extended address tracking, repeater address search and TopN groups are recommended. Extended tracking is for systems that can track the MAC addresses of several devices on one port, address search for systems that allow read-write access and can search all incoming data for an address, and TopN for systems with enough resources.
sections.eli5: Some parts of the control panel are required, some are required only for fancier boxes, and some are nice extras.
